questions.topic: What an argument array changes about a subprocess call
questions.learningObjective: Describe how passing arguments as a list changes a child process call.
questions.stem: The prep-list generator builds a recipe card by running a print utility, and the dish name is supplied as a list of separate strings instead of one joined string. Explain why that difference changes what the operating system does with the name.

answer.exemplar: Supplying the dish name as its own element of an argument array means the operating system hands the print utility exactly one argument containing spaces and punctuation, with no shell in between to re-read them. Joining the name into a single string and handing it to a shell lets the shell split it on spaces and act on characters such as semicolons or pipes as command separators, so a name like 'Lamb; remove everything' becomes a second command instead of a title.

questions.explanation: An argument array bypasses the shell, so each element arrives as one argument exactly as written. A joined string is re-parsed by a shell, which splits it and treats separators as syntax. That is why the array form is the safer default.
questions.hint: Ask whether a shell ever sees the name.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A link that passes a containment test
questions.learningObjective: State what a path comparison can and cannot decide.
questions.stem: A recipe card in the published folder points through a link to a file on the finance share, and the nightly check compares only path strings with the permitted directory. Which statement about that check is accurate?

options.text: It rejects the card, because a link is never a genuine recipe file
options.misconception: treats link type itself as the security failure

options.text: It passes the card and confirms the finance copy matches the kitchen one
options.misconception: assumes a path check compares file contents

options.text: It rejects the card, because the target sits outside the permitted folder
options.misconception: believes the check resolves targets before comparing

options.text: It passes the card while saying nothing about where the bytes live

questions.explanation: The check compares path strings, so it passes the card and never inspects the finance target. It says nothing about where the bytes live, and resolving the link first is what would change that.
questions.hint: Ask what the comparison actually read.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why a name-based test cannot see a link
questions.learningObjective: Measure how much of a library was truly examined.
questions.stem: A security review covered 640 named library entries, opened 430 of them and read their contents, and matched 210 by name alone. How much of the library was genuinely examined on content grounds?

options.text: 640 entries, since every name was matched against the approved list
options.misconception: counts name matching as content inspection

options.text: 430 entries, which is about two thirds of the 640 named items
210 entries, since only those were treated as unverified links
options.misconception: assumes the unexamined entries are all links

options.text: 0 entries, because no directory was crawled end to end
options.misconception: dismisses partial coverage as if it were zero coverage

questions.explanation: Only 430 entries were opened and read, so that is the real extent of content inspection, roughly two thirds of the library. The other 210 were judged on names alone, which reveals no content.
questions.hint: Count the entries that were opened.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A description that chooses which constructor runs
questions.learningObjective: Explain why resolving type first still matters for safety.
questions.stem: Each technique prefix such as 'cure:' is resolved to a class before any values from the row are used, and that ordering has a consequence for the safety of the import. Explain what that ordering means.

answer.exemplar: Resolving the type first means the class is chosen before any of the row's values are read, so a hostile value cannot pick the class, but a hostile prefix can. The prefix comes from a cell an ordinary user can edit, which makes the mapping table a place where a user can choose which code runs on their own data. The safe arrangement is a small reviewed mapping with no user-extensible entries, not a reliance on values being clean.

questions.explanation: Resolving the type first fixes which class runs before values are read, so values cannot choose the class, but the prefix still can, and users can edit that prefix in a cell.
questions.hint: Ask who controls the prefix.

questions.topic: Why reconstruction is more than parsing
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the objects built from a batch of rows.
questions.stem: A costing row contains 5 fields and the importer builds 8 objects from it. A batch of 11 identical rows is imported in one pass. How many objects does the whole batch build?
questions.explanation: Each row builds 8 objects, so 11 rows build 88 objects, since the row shape does not change. Multiplying the 5 fields instead of the 8 objects is the tempting error.
questions.hint: Objects per row times the number of rows.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What an argument array changes about a subprocess call
questions.learningObjective: Explain what an argument array does to a title's characters.

stimulus.body: During a kitchen systems test, a dish title was set to a value containing a shell command separator. With the old joined-string call the separator worked and a second command ran. With the new argument-array call the same title arrived as one argument and the separator did nothing.

questions.stem: Given this test note, what does the argument-array form change about the title's characters?

options.text: They are escaped, so the separator becomes harmless punctuation
options.misconception: credits escaping rather than the absence of a shell

options.text: They stay literal argument text, because nothing interprets them
They are removed, so the printer receives a shortened title
options.misconception: thinks the array form sanitises the text

options.text: They are executed, but only by the printer instead of the shell
options.misconception: assumes the same interpreter simply moved

questions.explanation: With the array form no shell reads the title, so its characters are never parsed as syntax and simply travel inside one argument. Nothing is escaped or stripped, and no interpreter moved.
questions.hint: Ask whether anything still reads the text.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The property an argument list gives a subprocess call
questions.learningObjective: Compare argument counts for the array and shell forms.
questions.stem: A prep-list command is built in two ways for the same dish. Stage one: the title is one element of an argument array, so the child receives it as a single argument. Stage two: the title is concatenated into a string that a shell reads, and it contains 5 words plus a shell separator. How many arguments does the child receive in stage two?

options.text: Five, because the shell drops the separator from the count
options.misconception: believes a separator is a word the shell counts

options.text: One, because the whole line still reaches the program as a single string
options.misconception: assumes a shell forwards its input line untouched

options.text: Seven, because the shell adds one argument for the separator itself
options.misconception: counts a shell separator as a delivered argument

options.text: Six, since the shell splits the five words and treats the separator as syntax

questions.explanation: In stage two the shell splits the line into words and treats the separator as syntax, so the child sees five word arguments instead of stage one's single title argument.
questions.hint: Count the words, and remember the separator is not text.
